name: Bakuchiol

card.summary: A plant-derived 'retinol alternative' for wrinkles and pigmentation, with a handful of small trials suggesting retinol-like results and less irritation.
card.aka: Babchi oil component, Psoralea corylifolia extract, 'plant retinol'
card.note: Few and small trials; head-to-head evidence against retinol is limited and mostly cosmetic-industry studies.

quick.overview:
Bakuchiol is a phenolic compound extracted mainly from the seeds of Psoralea corylifolia (babchi), used in Ayurvedic and Chinese medicine. It has no structural similarity to retinoids, but has been marketed as a gentler functional alternative to retinol in anti-aging creams and serums.

A systematic review of dermatology studies found 16 preclinical and seven clinical studies, mostly on photoaging, acne and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, with results described as comparable to topical retinoids. Evidence base is small and not large-scale.
quick.mechanism: Gene-expression studies reported that bakuchiol regulates many of the same genes as retinol, supporting collagen and epidermal renewal, without acting through retinoid receptors. It also has antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and antibacterial properties in lab studies.
quick.risks: Reviews say it lacks the burning and scaling commonly seen with topical retinoids, but one systematic review also notes a report of adverse events. Product labels advise avoiding eyes, stopping if irritation occurs and not applying to broken skin. It shows estrogen-receptor activity in lab studies, whose clinical meaning in skin products is not established.

lead: Bakuchiol is a meroterpene phenol obtained mainly from the seeds of Psoralea corylifolia, a plant used in traditional Indian and Chinese medicine for conditions such as psoriasis and leprosy [5][4]. It has become a cosmetic ingredient promoted as a 'retinol alternative' for photoaging, wrinkles, hyperpigmentation and acne [3].

Despite having no structural resemblance to retinoids, bakuchiol was reported in a 2014 study to regulate gene expression similarly to retinol [12]. A 2019 randomized, double-blind trial in the British Journal of Dermatology compared topical bakuchiol with retinol for facial photoageing [6]. A 2022 systematic review of 30 articles, 16 of them preclinical and seven clinical, concluded that results in photoaging, acne and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation were comparable to retinoids, while observing that the clinical evidence is small [3].

paras: Bakuchiol is used in facial serums and moisturizers for anti-aging, evening of skin tone and sensitive skin, sometimes alongside other actives such as melatonin, ascorbyl derivatives, genistein, GABA or DMAE [9][11][8][20]. Reviews describe studies for acne, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and wrinkles [5]. Its anti-inflammatory and anti-proliferative properties have prompted laboratory interest in psoriasis and skin cancer, with the review noting more clinical evidence is needed [5].

A 2014 study using gene expression profiling reported that bakuchiol shares functional effects with retinol despite a different structure [12]. Laboratory studies describe antioxidant, antibacterial, anti-inflammatory and estrogen-like effects [4][17]. Phytoestrogen work on P. corylifolia constituents has examined estrogen-receptor subtype selectivity [16]. A 2024 study reported that bakuchiol targets mitochondrial proteins such as prohibitins and voltage-dependent anion channels in antiviral research [13].

A 2019 randomized, double-blind, controlled trial compared topical bakuchiol and retinol for facial photoageing, assessing efficacy and side-effects [6]; a registered trial of 44 participants compared their cosmetic effects on wrinkles and photoaging [18]. The 2022 systematic review described benefits comparable to retinoids across studies of photodamage, hyperpigmentation, wrinkle scores and acne severity, noting that many studies tested bakuchiol in combination products [3].

Other studies include a trial of a nature-based bakuchiol moisturizer in sensitive skin [9], a clinical evaluation of a serum with melatonin, bakuchiol and ascorbyl tetraisopalmitate [11], a 2026 randomized trial of a genistein plus bakuchiol and vitamins product on male facial skin [8], and a trichloroacetic acid model of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation [10]. Registered studies cover post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (n=22), acne with ethyl linoleate (n=40) and split-face comparisons of retinol alternatives [19][21][22]. A 2025 study of a Silybum marianum extract compared a different retinol alternative with retinol [7]. A 2024 systematic review of cosmeceuticals for anti-aging also covers the area [2].
The published literature describe the overall evidence as limited by small samples and by the use of multi-ingredient products.

Reviews report that bakuchiol does not cause the burning and scaling common with topical retinoids, which has led to its use in sensitive skin [5]. The 2022 systematic review included one report on adverse events among the studies it identified [3]. A US product label for a bakuchiol serum advises external use only, avoiding eye contact, stopping if redness, itching or irritation develops, and not applying to broken or irritated skin [23].

Psoralea corylifolia has a long history in Ayurvedic, Chinese and Korean medicine, per reviews and an encyclopedic summary [15][1]. Bakuchiol was isolated as a constituent in earlier natural-product work, including studies of DNA polymerase inhibitors in 1998 [14]. It was characterized as a retinol-like functional compound in cosmetic research published in 2014 [12]. The first total synthesis of the racemic compound was reported in 1967, according to an encyclopedic summary [1].
